title: Check Token: Real-Time Self-Verification and Precise Truncation in LLM Reasoning
summary:
arXiv:2611.18564v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: ECC memory embeds 8 parity bits for every 64 data bits and automatically detects and corrects errors on each read. The parity bits carry no data and only safeguard integrity, at ~12.5% overhead. Yet the reasoning chains of large language models lack such built-in self-verification: once an error occurs it propagates along the chain, and existing methods can only verify externally after generation completes. We propose the check token, establishing built-in self-verification for language model generation streams for the first time: a functional marker  is added to the vocabulary, and the model triggers self-checking (analysis, localization, truncation, rewriting) by outputting it at any position. The check token carries no reasoning content (discarded after triggering) and only safeguards reasoning correctness, directly corresponding to the role of ECC parity bits, also at only ~13% overhead. Speculative forking further eliminates false-positive latency, and segmented reward makes trigger timing end-to-end learnable. Experiments (Qwen3-32B / Qwen3-Next) show that the check token achieves +10.8 pp improvement on HMMT25 at 1.13x overhead, with token efficiency 88x that of Best-of-8, and the precise truncation advantage monotonically increases with chain length.

title: Quantize, Qualify, Rerank: A Recipe for Compressing LLMs Without Losing Quality
summary:
arXiv:2611.18587v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Compressing large language models lowers serving cost, but a single automatic metric may miss quality loss. For the WMT26 Model Compression constrained track, we compress google/gemma-3-12b-it (24.4 GB in bf16) for three translation directions on one H100. Paired bootstrap analysis exposes metric disagreement on 4-bit quantization; guided by WMT24 human meta-evaluation, we use MetricX24-XXL as primary and CometKiwi-XXL as a cross-check. Removing the unused vision stack and non-task vocabulary and using int8 weights or fp8 activations causes no resolved loss, whereas int4 leaves a small residual. QLoRA healing overfits its calibration domain. A Cometoid best-of-4 reranker at $T=0.3$ improves both the 8-bit and 4-bit systems under WMT25 test set. On post-submission WMT26, both remain competitive with bf16 under reference-free metrics; the small difference between the reranked variants is treated as noise.

title: Skill-Latent Rewards: LLM-Guided Reward Formulation for Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
summary:
arXiv:2611.18597v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon reinforcement learning under sparse and delayed feedback remains an open challenge. Existing return-decomposition methods redistribute episodic rewards to ease credit assignment, but they operate on raw state--action transitions and disregard the subgoal structure that governs meaningful progress in complex tasks. We propose Skill-LR, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework in which a vision--language model identifies the agent's active subgoal at each timestep and a large language model generates a matching latent reward formulation through a two-stage prompting process. By conditioning reward signals on the currently active subgoal, Skill-LR produces stage-specific credit that evolves with the hierarchical plan, reducing temporal variance and improving sample efficiency. On multi-stage MiniGrid and BabyAI benchmarks, including DoorKey and Unlock-to-Unlock, Skill-LR converges faster and more reliably than sparse environmental rewards and strong credit-assignment baselines such as RUDDER and LaRe, demonstrating that subgoal-aligned latent rewards offer a principled path toward stable, interpretable credit assignment in long-horizon tasks.

title: Not All Data Leakage Is Equal: A Controlled Benchmark of Evaluation Inflation in Tabular Classification
summary:
arXiv:2611.18598v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Data leakage is widely recognized as a threat to trustworthy machine-learning evaluation, yet the phrase covers mechanisms with very different statistical consequences. We present a controlled empirical benchmark that measures the inflation in held-out ROC-AUC caused by five common leakage mechanisms: global standardization, global median imputation, duplicate contamination, supervised feature selection before splitting, and target encoding before splitting. The benchmark spans six public datasets and two synthetic stress tests, three model families, and five repeated stratified train/test splits, yielding 600 paired clean-versus-leaked comparisons. To avoid pseudo-replication, inference is performed on dataset-level effects with cluster bootstrap confidence intervals and Holm-corrected one-sided Wilcoxon tests. Label-dependent or direct data-reuse mechanisms produced systematic optimism: global target encoding increased ROC-AUC by 2.42 percentage points on average (95% cluster-bootstrap CI 0.62--4.89), global supervised feature selection by 1.93 points (0.63--3.39), and duplicate contamination by 1.52 points (0.40--2.80). All three remained significant after multiplicity correction. In contrast, global scaling and global median imputation had near-zero average effects under the i.i.d. settings studied here. A controlled target-encoding stress test further shows that leakage becomes sharply worse as categories become sparse. The results support a severity-aware view of leakage: evaluation pipelines should prevent all held-out-data dependence, but label-dependent transformations and observation reuse deserve especially aggressive auditing.

event_model_payload.title: Not All Data Leakage Is Equal: A Controlled Benchmark of Evaluation Inflation in Tabular Classification

title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Mambas Selective Gate in Financial Markets: A Leakage-Controlled Study
summary:
arXiv:2611.18599v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Selectively gated state-space models (SSMs), notably Mamba, are increasingly used for financial time series, yet how they internally represent market regimes (bull, bear, sideways) remains opaque. This paper applies Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) to a six-layer Mamba trained on approximately twenty-one years of daily data for a point-in-time set of S&P 500 constituents plus macroeconomic and Fama-French factors, decomposing per-layer hidden states with Top-K Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). Our central contribution is methodological and cautionary. A prior, uncontrolled configuration recovered market regimes from SAE features at F1 = 1.00. Under a controlled protocol that (i) removes the three input features that overlap the HMM label definition, (ii) disables the auxiliary regime-classification head, (iii) uses a point-in-time constituent universe, and (iv) evaluates against labels disjoint from the inputs, the same regime label is recovered at only F1 = 0.398, indistinguishable from a logistic baseline on raw inputs (0.435) and from an SAE trained on a randomly initialized, untrained Mamba (0.364). A 2x2 attribution grid shows the near-perfect result is an interaction of auxiliary supervision and label-defining inputs: neither factor alone exceeds F1 ~ 0.40. Effect sizes with block-bootstrap inference show the residual selective-gate (Delta t) regime effect is statistically detectable but economically negligible and uniform across layers rather than layer-specialized; the apparent polysemanticity gradient disappears under continuous, theory-grounded measures. We contribute a reproducible leakage-control protocol for interpretability evaluation of financial SSMs, a quantified demonstration that previously reported regime structure is a label-contamination artifact, and a modest economically grounded feature subset that genuinely survives the controls.

title: Multimodal Fusion with Pre-trained Models for Psychotherapy Outcome Prediction from Emotional Dynamics
summary:
arXiv:2611.18635v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In-session emotional dynamics are associated with psychotherapy outcomes but difficult to measure at scale. Pretrained multimodal models provide automated access to facial, vocal, and textual signals, yet clinical datasets remain small. Our research question is how pretrained multimodal representations can best support psychotherapy outcome prediction under data scarcity. Three studies use 106 sessions from 88 patients and nine session-level outcome scales (HSCL-11, EPO-1, POMS). Study 1 asks whether deep learning outperforms classical machine learning: a two-stage deep pipeline, first predicting window-level valence/arousal and then session outcomes, transferred poorly (best single configuration, $r=.078$). Study 2 asks which representation and preprocessing choices work best: statistical pooling of frozen pretrained embeddings with regularized classical models achieved average $r=.406$ across nine scales under per-scale configuration selection, up to $r=.490$ for symptom distress, with complementary modalities and no significant benefit from manual affect annotations or therapist features. Study 3 asks whether deep learning remains inferior under these choices: classical models outperformed an optimized single-stage deep model at the single-configuration level ($r=.281$ vs. $.222$) and on all nine scales under matched per-scale selection ($.406$ vs. $.252$). The results suggest that under clinical data scarcity, pretrained representations with fixed statistical pooling and regularized classical models are more reliable than learned aggregation.

title: Predictive maintenance in manufacturing: The operational value of continual machine learning
summary:
arXiv:2611.18636v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Predictive maintenance in high-volume manufacturing often faces a domain-incremental learning problem: as new product configurations enter production, prediction models must learn from newly available data while preserving performance on earlier configurations that remain in operation. In this paper, we empirically study the operational value of continual machine learning methods for addressing this challenge in predictive maintenance, using real-world maintenance data from Bosch. The setting at Bosch covers 25 product configurations over five years, which creates a practical challenge for predictive maintenance models, as such models must be updated with data from newly introduced configurations without reducing performance on configurations learned earlier, a phenomenon known as "forgetting". At the same time, retaining all historical sensor data and repeatedly retraining models is often infeasible in high-volume manufacturing since industrial machines generate too large data volumes. To address this challenge, we combine continual machine learning with robust optimization to support predictive maintenance. We then compare continual machine learning with a broad set of baselines, including fine-tuning, domain-adaptation methods, online learning methods, and configuration-specific models. Across experiments, continual machine learning methods achieve stronger predictive performance and lower maintenance costs than the baselines, with a reduction of cost-related indicators of more than 40 % relative to the baselines. Our results demonstrate the operational value of continual machine learning for decision support in maintenance when product portfolios grow over time and historical manufacturing data cannot be fully retained.

title: GRAFT: Cross-Backbone LoRA Reuse for Continual Language and Multimodal Learning
summary:
arXiv:2611.18638v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In continual learning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning enables large language models to acquire new capabilities through lightweight adapters such as LoRA, yet the reuse of pretrained adapters is typically restricted to models sharing the same backbone. This limits the transfer of learned capabilities from language models to multimodal models. We propose GRAFT (Generalist Reuse of Adapters via Feature-space Transfer), a framework for cross-backbone LoRA reuse. GRAFT retrieves the most relevant pretrained LoRA adapter from a modality-aware library and maps it into the target backbone through a learned linear bridge between corresponding source and target feature spaces. We evaluate GRAFT on ten Super-NaturalInstructions text tasks, transferring Qwen2.5 LoRAs to Qwen2.5-VL, and five multimodal tasks, where Qwen2.5-VL LoRAs are directly reused. Compared with randomly initialized LoRA adapters, GRAFT improves performance on most evaluated tasks. These results show that GRAFT provides a simple and effective mechanism for reusing learned capabilities across language and multimodal models in continual learning.

title: SynthDCB: World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking
summary:
arXiv:2611.18639v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both the worlds agents interact with and the tasks they must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a scalable benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation. World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, interaction constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components, which are composed into interactive worlds with explicit states, actions, and temporal dynamics. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis, allowing new capabilities to enter evaluation through a shared construction pipeline. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone domains with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. The stateful design enables task validation and agent evaluation through state correctness and tool-call traces. We evaluate seven models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 68.2% Pass@1. Error analysis reveals challenges in answer delivery, feasibility diagnosis, and temporal coordination. Construction experiments demonstrate scalability across domains and token efficiency: world distillation reduces token consumption by 0.9-66.0% and 46.2-92.5% relative to Codex with low and xhigh reasoning effort, respectively, while achieving broader capability coverage. SynthDCB makes executable world construction the basis of scalable device-control benchmarking, connecting an expanding space of capabilities and interactions to verifiable agent evaluation.

title: SERAG: SEmantical and Relational approach for Anomaly detection on knowledge Graphs
summary:
arXiv:2611.18640v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Knowledge graphs constructed from text can contain facts that are individually plausible yet inconsistent with their relational context. We introduce SERAG, a supervised anomaly detector that combines two complementary plausibility estimates: a semantic score computed from separately encoded subject, relation, and object labels, and a relational score obtained through a relational graph convolutional network. The scores are standardized, calibrated, and fused. We evaluate the method on a subset of ICEWS18 with vocabulary-constrained synthetic anomalies generated by an LLM, using pooled and chronological splits. At 10% anomaly prevalence, SERAG achieves test AUPRCs of 0.321 and 0.258, respectively, compared with 0.159 and 0.146 for the strongest adapted baseline. Fusion improves mean test AUPRC over either branch alone, with a larger gain in the pooled protocol and a smaller validation-selected gain in the chronological protocol. Additional anomaly supervision improves performance. These results support the complementarity of textual and relational signals for detecting synthetic anomalies under the evaluated protocols.

title: HIMX: mixed-format matrix multiplication based on customized HIFLOAT4 representations
summary:
arXiv:2611.18641v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: 4-bit weight-activation quantization (W4A4) is an important approach for efficient large language model (LLM) inference. Recent hierarchical formats such as HiFloat4 (HIF4) improve the representational range of 4-bit quantization through multi-level scaling. However, the same local mantissa representation in HIF4 may not be equally suitable for weights and activations, which exhibit distinct distribution characteristics. To address this limitation, we propose HiMX, a mixed-mantissa framework built upon the hierarchical scaling structure of HIF4. Our key observation is that the two HIF4-compatible mantissa representations, S1P2 and E2M1, exhibit complementary quantization behavior: the denser S1P2 format provides higher resolution for concentrated weight distributions, while the wider-spaced E2M1 format provides complementary quantization characteristics for activation tensors. HiMX enables operand-tailored mantissa representations while converting heterogeneous mantissas into fixed-point integer operands with operand-specific widths, allowing different operand formats to share a unified integer multiply-accumulate (MAC) array. Block-level analysis on Qwen3-8B shows that HIF4-S1P2 is better suited for weights while HIF4 E2M1 is better suited for activations, and their mixed-format combination achieves lower output MSE than homogeneous configurations. Across multiple benchmarks, HiMX reduces the average end-to-end accuracy loss from 2.38 to 1.77 points on Qwen3-8B and from 2.23 to 1.85 points on Qwen3-30B-A3B, demonstrating the potential benefit of heterogeneous mantissa representations for W4A4 LLM inference.

title: FedFit: Federated Dynamic Sparse Training via Fisher Information scoring
summary:
arXiv:2611.18643v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cross-device Federated Learning (FL) is frequently bottlenecked by the prohibitive memory and communication costs of training deep neural networks on resource-constrained edge hardware. While federated dynamic sparse training aims to alleviate these costs by adjusting sparse structures during training, existing methods rely on magnitude-based heuristics that are fundamentally ill-suited for the non-convergent, heterogeneous environments inherent to FL. To address this challenge, we propose FedFit, a federated dynamic sparse training framework that replaces simple heuristics with optimization-centric criteria for structure adjustment. By leveraging a second-order approximation of the loss landscape via the Fisher Information Matrix, FedFit enables precise and efficient structure adjustment without the overhead of explicit Hessian computation. Empirical evaluations across computer vision and natural language processing benchmarks demonstrate that FedFit significantly narrows the sparse-to-dense accuracy gap, outperforming state-of-the-art methods while maintaining high communication efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/Serena-28/Fedfit.git .

event_model_payload.title: FedFit: Federated Dynamic Sparse Training via Fisher Information scoring

title: Minari: Infrastructure for Collaborative Reinforcement Learning Datasets
summary:
arXiv:2611.18644v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) depends on shared datasets, but sharing them is still hard. Each benchmark ships its own format, documentation is thin, and most datasets cannot be regenerated once the environment code moves on. We introduce Minari, an open-source Python library for creating, sharing, and loading RL datasets. Its API follows Gymnasium, so recording a dataset means wrapping an environment and stepping through it as usual. From there, users can attach metadata, filter, combine, and shuffle datasets, and publish or download them with one command through the HuggingFace Hub. Every dataset stores the environment specification, seeds, applied wrappers, and pinned package requirements needed to rebuild the environment and regenerate the data. TorchRL, AgileRL, and d3rlpy already load Minari datasets natively, so switching datasets in those libraries takes one line of code. Minari also hosts 338 reproducible datasets (350K trajectories, 55M steps) covering robotic locomotion and manipulation, maze and grid navigation, language-conditioned instruction following, Atari, and web navigation, including a full regeneration of D4RL with public generation scripts. We report baseline scores for six offline RL algorithms on the regenerated D4RL and MuJoCo datasets.

title: RSIMed: Scaling Medical Foundation Models beyond Limited Clinical Data via Retrieval-Grounded Self-Evolution
summary:
arXiv:2611.18646v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rare diseases are hard to diagnose, and the labeled clinical records needed to train models for them are few, private, and slow to extend, since a specialist must read every case. A model that writes its own training tasks could learn beyond these records, but no program can check a model-written diagnosis, and a wrong answer key corrupts training. To tackle this dilemma between data scarcity and difficulty of data annotations, we introduce RSIMed, Recursive Self-Improvement in Medicine, one of the first self-evolving pipelines in which a task proposer co-evolves in context with a diagnostic solver on real clinical records. Seeded by training admissions, a frozen copy of the solver writes each clinical question from retrieved medical evidence, so its answer rests on a source, and steers topics and difficulty toward what the solver still gets wrong. On rare-disease diagnosis from MIMIC-IV admissions, the accuracy of RSIMed-27B grows linearly with training compute, while a static pool of generated tasks collapses. Without any external model, RSIMed-27B and RSIMed-9B reach 0.516 and 0.488 diagnostic accuracy, above every off-the-shelf GPT-5.6 setting, whose best reaches 0.399 at 38 times the inference cost of RSIMed-27B. Tasks written by four external teachers, including GPT-5.5, train a less accurate diagnostician than the solver's own. Trained only on diagnosis, RSIMed-RL-27B also improves on the physician-written tasks of HealthBench Professional, from 0.291 to 0.303 in adjusted score.

title: Screen Before You Add: Reducing Candidate Inference in Model Ensembles
summary:
arXiv:2611.18647v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As new models become available, existing ensembles must be updated to be competitive, making them intrinsically dynamic. Deciding whether to add a candidate model can require inference on an entire annotated dataset. Such a screening becomes prohibitive for models with costly inference especially when they ultimately add no value. Even under simple convex aggregation, relying on benchmark scores can be misleading as strong standalone performance does not guarantee ensemble improvement, and fitted ensemble weights can hurt test performance. In this work, we study candidate screening and show how early rejection can be achieved safely, exploiting residual geometry for stratification and rejecting the candidate when the best possible remaining predictions cannot achieve the necessary improvement. The key result that justifies this approach is that, under convex aggregation and squared or Brier loss, the population optimum improves if and only if a candidate induces a prediction change positively aligned with the residuals of the population-optimal existing ensemble. An optimistic quadratic program (QP) provides certified early rejection, while posterior-scenario sampling offers an alternative heuristic. We evaluate the approach by showing the tradeoff between saved calls and screening accuracy, which refers to recovering the same accept/reject result as for the entire annotated dataset. We assess empirically whether full-dataset decisions predict candidate usefulness on a held-out test set. On two LLM panels, stratified screening with certified QP rejection saves 21-23% of candidate calls while keeping 100% screening accuracy. In our experiments, sampling posterior scenarios further increases call savings to approximately 37%, with a loss of less than one percentage point in screening accuracy.

title: Rethinking Offline On-Policy Distillation: From Scalar Advantages to Distributional Supervision
summary:
arXiv:2611.18648v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher capabilities through token-level feedback on student-generated trajectories, but repeatedly evaluating fresh rollouts with the teacher is computationally expensive. Offline methods such as Lightning OPD reduce this cost by caching recorded tokens' teacher log-probabilities on fixed reference rollouts. By extending the idea to a multi-turn agentic search setup, we find that it consistently underperforms the SFT starting point trained by the same teacher. We empirically observe greater teacher--reference mismatch than in mathematical reasoning and post-training distributional flattening, and theoretically show that scalar advantage supervision on fixed rollouts admits solutions with flattened output distributions under suitable conditions. Motivated by these findings, we propose Distributional On-Policy Distillation (DistOPD), a simple yet effective offline OPD method that retains candidate-token probabilities from both reference and teacher at selected positions and aggregates the remaining parts into a residual token. On agentic search, DistOPD achieves performance comparable to online OPD while improving student--teacher alignment and using training GPU-hours comparable to Lightning OPD.

title: Algebraic Interaction: A Recipe for Neural Architecture Generation
summary:
arXiv:2611.18649v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce an algebraic foundation for neural architecture design in which convolution, attention, state-space models, and equivariant layers are expressed through compositions of bilinear product operators over two structures: a position algebra governing positional routing and a feature algebra governing feature interactions. This decomposition makes routing, feature algebra, and operator composition explicit design variables.We focus on the feature-algebra axis through an Algebraic Recipe: fix the routing and operator composition of an existing architecture while replacing its feature algebra. This preserves the information-flow structure while allowing computational and symmetry properties to be modified through algebraic specification.We instantiate the recipe in linear attention, Mamba, and equivariant networks. Structure-constant and Clifford algebras improve accuracy at comparable parameter count in linear attention; structure-constant algebras yield up to $3\times$ faster training and inference in Vision Mamba at competitive accuracy; and an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-representation algebra provides rotational equivariance by construction. These results demonstrate that feature algebra alone can control accuracy, efficiency, and symmetry without redesigning positional routing.This turns algebraic structure into an explicit design variable and reduces architecture design, within our framework, to algebraic specification.

title: MeltKV: Memory-Aligned KV Cache Compression via Variable-Bit Packed Vector Quantization for Long-Context LLMs
summary:
arXiv:2611.18652v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on long contexts, making Key-Value (KV) caches dominate memory usage and inference latency. Existing vector quantization (VQ) methods effectively compress KV caches to sub-4-bit levels but often overlook inefficiencies in memory alignment and decoding speed. This work introduces MeltKV, a memory-latency co-optimized KV cache quantization framework for long-context LLM serving. MeltKV employs a memory-aligned variable-bit index packing scheme that adaptively assigns bit-widths to grouped key channels and compactly stores indices within standard data-types, eliminating redundant bits. Additionally, head-wise codebook sharing reduces the total codebook size while maintaining accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that MeltKV effectively compresses KV representations to sub-4-bit levels down to 1 bit and, at comparable perplexity, achieves 48.1% lower memory usage and 52.9% lower latency than state-of-the-art VQ methods.

title: Earth World Model: Physics-constrained latent dynamics for forecasting and environmental scenario analysis
summary:
arXiv:2611.18654v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World models have been widely applied to multi-agent planning and forecasting, but exogenous environmental changes are rarely incorporated as replaceable drivers in a unified state-evolution process. This limits assessment of whether environmental perturbations propagate through physical systems with faithful dynamics. We propose the Earth World Model (EWM), an Earth-centred forecasting framework that compresses heterogeneous multi-source observations into a reusable low-dimensional latent state representing the system's history and current condition. Given explicit exogenous drivers, a shared transition operator recursively updates the latent state, and physics-constrained decoding produces multi-step forecasts. Replacing the drivers enables environmental scenario analysis and evaluation of dynamic-response fidelity. We evaluated EWM for power forecasting and environmental-perturbation response at six photovoltaic sites and one wind-power site. Across four photovoltaic sites and three forecast horizons, three independent training runs yielded mean $R^2$ values of 0.8578-0.9095. In a separate six-site decoder ablation, the mean net per-unit response $\rho$ under the prescribed irradiance intervention increased from 0.180 with a multilayer perceptron decoder to 0.922 with an analytic physical decoder, close to site- and horizon-specific analytic references. The wind model achieved an injection elasticity of $0.9990 \pm 0.0006$, while pre-intervention outputs remained unchanged. These results show that forecast fit and intervention response should be evaluated separately and that the tested EWM configurations preserved response amplitude and temporal boundaries under the prescribed interventions.

title: Beveridge: Open Weight System One Decision Models with Calibrated Probabilities
summary:
arXiv:2611.18655v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many production systems need a model to make a narrow decision about a document (route a ticket, check a limit, refuse a request, pick the next step of a browser agent) rather than to write text about it. We present Beveridge, a family of open weight System One decision models that take a document and up to 15 typed questions (yes/no, choice among described options, or a level on an ordered scale) and return, in one forward pass without generating text, an answer with a calibrated probability for every option. Beveridge-Large-C (398M parameters) adds a 3.5M parameter decision network to ModernBERT-large: typed number and date features in the input, exact facts from a rule engine, question-to-document evidence attention, a three-step recursive core with learned halting and an exact yes/no path. Beveridge-Pro-C adapts Gemma 4 26B-A4B with LoRA to score option letters, and Beveridge-Pro-C-Web extends it to the next step of a browser agent. On held-out tests the 0.4B model reaches 93.0% on our operations-document benchmark against 91.1% for the best of five general LLMs (31B-675B) and 87.9% for a commercial System One API, and, because its confidences are calibrated (ECE 0.029 on that benchmark), it can hand over 76% of decisions automatically at 95% accuracy, where no general LLM we tested can hand over any. It answers in 4.9 ms per decision on one NVIDIA H200 GPU and 60 ms on the 14 core CPU of an Apple M4 Pro laptop. Beveridge-Pro-C-Web raises next-step accuracy on web pages from unseen site types from 49.4% to 98.2% and completes live browsing tasks without losing document accuracy. We describe the models, the training recipes and an evaluation on 19 held-out test sets against a commercial System One API and five general LLMs, including where the models are weak. Weights and inference code are released under Apache 2.0.

title: ECOD: Experience-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Turn Agents
summary:
arXiv:2611.18656v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse and delayed rewards make reinforcement learning challenging for long-horizon language agents. On-policy distillation (OPD) complements environmental rewards with dense teacher feedback on student-generated contexts. Standard OPD can misalign supervision with relative teacher competence, student trajectory outcomes, and the temporal structure of task execution. Recent variants adjust guidance through divergence-based weighting and temporal schedules, while joint calibration from task-completion experience remains underexplored. We introduce Experience-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation (ECOD), which allocates teacher supervision at the task, trajectory, and turn levels. ECOD compares teacher and student success-rate posteriors under matched task conditions, restricts direct supervision to failed student trajectories, and derives a temporal prior from successful teacher lengths. The resulting weight applies to teacher losses or teacher-derived advantages. We evaluate ECOD on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Under matched teacher settings, ECOD improves standard OPD by up to 4.06% in relative ALFWorld unseen success. Across both model scales, ECOD-assisted SOD, TCOD-F2B, and ATOD configurations yield average paired relative gains of 6.20% on ALFWorld unseen and 7.05% on WebShop, with WebShop gains ranging from 2.29% to 21.60%. These results support experience-calibrated supervision allocation as a reusable mechanism across distinct distillation objectives.

event_model_payload.title: ECOD: Experience-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Turn Agents

title: SART: Sign-Absolute Reformulation Theory for Binary Variable Reduction in Neural Network Verification
summary:
arXiv:2611.18657v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Complete formal verification of neural networks is crucial for their deployment in safety-critical domains. A key bottleneck stems from encoding complexity: traditional methods assign one binary variable per unstable ReLU neuron. We propose the Sign-Absolute Reformulation Theory (SART), which fundamentally breaks the conventional one-to-one mapping between unstable neurons and binary variables by establishing formal reducibility criteria. This allows for finer-grained modeling, where each unstable neuron corresponds on average to fewer than one binary variable, thereby reducing verification complexity at its source. Based on SART, we derive a theoretical lower bound on the number of binary variables required for complete verification and, under the assumption that $P \neq NP$, prove that variables in the final layer can be compressed by 50\%, while the number of variables in intermediate layers cannot be further reduced. To overcome the apparent ``last-layer-only'' limitation, we recast verification as a sequential process and, crucially, show that the gain lifts to the entire network: LayerABS, a SART-based progressive tightening verifier, iteratively treats intermediate layers as temporary final layers and propagates tight bounds that shrink the global search space and binary-variable counts. Furthermore, we reveal a structural law influencing verification complexity: when the signs of weights of unstable neurons satisfy numerical symmetry, with positive and negative weights equal or differing by at most one, the worst-case verification complexity achieves the theoretical optimum, offering theoretical guidance for the design of verification-friendly architectures. As a general-purpose underlying encoding, the value of SART is independent of specific algorithms.

title: Rethinking the Verification of Machine Unlearning
summary:
arXiv:2611.18658v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine unlearning claims require evidence that a model has removed the influence of specified training data. Yet widely deployable post hoc verifiers. infer unlearning largely from predictive behavior, the final model response that remains under the provider's control. We make this limitation concrete through Output-Level Deceptive Response (ODR), an attack that produces responses accepted by output based verifiers while preserving the original representation state. By separating output conformity from internal unlearning, ODR motivates a rethinking of machine unlearning verification, shifting the audit target from what the model returns to what changes inside it. We operationalize this shift through Representation Unlearning Verification (RUV), a gray box verifier that compares intermediate forward representations in the original and unlearned models. RUV traces a four-stage response through activation reorganization, representation displacement, neighborhood disruption, and loss of manifold support. Matched retained controls distinguish target specific responses from global model drift, while joint permutation calibration combines the four evidence views into an adaptive decision. Experiments spanning exact and approximate unlearning, class and sample level requests, multiple datasets, and diverse architectures show mean ODR deception success rates of $97.0\%$ and $97.7\%$, respectively. RUV achieves mean verification accuracies of $98.9\%$ and $94.9\%$, while rejecting $99.5\%$ and $99.8\%$ of the corresponding ODR submissions.

title: Stagewise Adaptive Boosting
summary:
arXiv:2611.18662v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Stagewise algorithms and sparsity-inducing regularization are two influential approaches to high-dimensional modeling. Existing stagewise theory, however, largely centers on convex regularization, whereas stronger sparsity and other structural preferences are often pursued through fixed-level nonconvex optimization rather than generating an entire adaptive solution path. We develop stagewise adaptive boosting, a general framework that builds a monotone path by selecting the update consistent with structural preference. The framework can encourage sparsity along the path itself and also admits extensions that promote other properties of the solution, including group selection, similarity across models for multiple outcomes, and known priorities or prerequisite relations among predictors. We study its theoretical property as well as finite sample performance using simulations and real-data analyses. Across these studies, the proposed pathwise approach often achieves predictive performance comparable to commonly used baselines while selecting substantially smaller models. These results suggest that adaptive stagewise learning provides a practical route to stronger sparsity and richer structural control without repeatedly solving separate weighted or nonconvex optimization problems.

title: Can a Vision-Language Model Tune Clustering In Context?
summary:
arXiv:2611.18768v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clustering is a widely used unsupervised learning method, but selecting an appropriate algorithm and set of hyperparameters for a specific dataset can require many possible configurations and evaluations. In this work, we investigate whether a Vision-Language Model can instead visually evaluate clustering results and use those decisions to then tune an explicit clustering algorithm. We study this through three progressive experiments using Qwen3.5-27B and five controlled synthetic clustering scenarios. First, we test whether the VLM can distinguish the best clustering result from a pair of plots. Second, we test whether it can assign numerical scores to those plots where a higher score represents a better result. Finally, we use these judgments within an agentic loop in which the VLM scores a k-means clustering and proposes updated hyperparameters that may result in better clustering. Our exploratory results show that the VLM performs well when clear cluster structure is present, while struggling on more ambiguous and noisy settings. In the full agentic experiment, the VLM produces clustering configurations with silhouette scores relatively close to those of grid search and Bayesian optimization, while terminating in much fewer iterations. Overall, these results provide an initial proof of concept that VLM-based visual feedback can be used to autonomously tune an explicit clustering algorithm.

title: Gradient-Guided Hardware-Native MIXFP4
summary:
arXiv:2611.18769v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Blackwell tensor cores support native inference with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4), but NVFP4 leaves a perplexity (PPL) gap to BF16. Choosing a format for each 16-element block can improve accuracy, but current matrix multiply instructions cannot execute choices this fine. Applying these rules at hardware-compatible tiles loses most of their benefit. We introduce FlipQuant, which selects E2M1 or E0M3 for each MMA weight tile. It keeps both quantized weight candidates fixed and learns a binary format map from end-to-end gradients of a bucketed KL loss to a BF16 teacher, re-evaluating them after each update. Native kernels execute 16 x 64 tiles on SM120 and 256 x 64 tiles on SM100 with median GEMM overheads of 1.9% and 1.7%, respectively. Across six language models and two corpora, FlipQuant at 16 x 64 closes 42.5% of NVFP4's PPL gap to BF16 on average, compared with 13.3% for FourOverSix. Code is available at https://github.com/brian030128/flipquant.

title: Setting Optimal Reserve Prices using Fine-Tuned Language Models
summary:
arXiv:2611.18785v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Online auction houses must set reserve prices for highly differentiated products whose unstructured descriptions contain valuable demand information. Existing approaches generally require managers to specify product attributes in advance. We ask whether a language model can instead learn from listing descriptions and historical bids to set item-specific reserve prices before bidding begins. We fine-tune a pretrained text embedding language model using the structural likelihood of auction bids as its training objective. This directs representation learning toward the valuation distribution that determines the reserve decision. We show that consecutive upper bids identify the tail information needed to set an optimal reserve without observing or modeling the number of potential bidders. A split-sample estimator learns the representation on one half of the data and conducts structural estimation and inference conditional on that representation on the other. We apply the method to approximately 65,800 online used-vehicle auctions. With seller values calibrated to match the sale rate among listings, the model implies a counterfactual net increase of $165.8 million, representing a 14.6% increase above the incumbent reserve policy. The framework translates a listing description and a seller's value into an item-specific reserve recommendation without constructing a product taxonomy or requiring a bid history for the item being priced. It provides an approach to adapting language models for operational decisions in marketplaces where products are heterogeneous and demand-relevant information is recorded in text.

title: Hybrid Compression for Memory-Efficient Matrix-Vector Multiplication
summary:
arXiv:2611.18792v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Iterative machine-learning algorithms repeatedly access large real-valued matrices through matrix-vector products, and their performance is limited by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic throughput. Lossless compression schemes that support computation directly over the compressed data reduce both the data moved and the memory footprint of these workloads. The mm-RePair framework [11] follows this approach by applying the RePair grammar compressor to the Compressed Sparse Row/Value (CSRV) representation of a matrix and performing matrix-vector multiplications directly on the compressed data. Its effectiveness, however, degrades on matrices that are dense or contain many distinct values. In this paper we present a hybrid strategy for the mm-RePair framework that combines grammar and entropy compression. The CSRV sequence is partitioned into a grammar-compressible component, formed by the entries that mm-RePair can compress effectively, and an entropy-compressible component holding the remaining entries, which is encoded with the ans-fold coder [24]. Compression improves further by sorting and delta encoding the entries of each row in the CSRV representation, and by remapping the alphabet to a contiguous range. Experiments on real-valued machine-learning matrices, including word embeddings and transformer hidden states, show that our hybrid strategy is more compact than the original \mmRepair on every input and reduces the peak memory of multiplication, with the largest gains on dense matrices with many distinct values, at competitive multiplication times. It also outperforms the column-reordering variant of \mmRepair on most of the matrices, and combining the two is even more compact on the sparse ones, at the cost of a much longer compression time. Finally, our strategy scales with the number of threads as well as the original \mmRepair does.

title: Actuarial-Informed Neural Networks: Constrained Deep Learning for Sex-Specific Multi-Population Longevity Forecasting
summary:
arXiv:2611.18802v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce Actuarial-Informed Neural Networks (AINN), a constrained deep learning framework for sex-specific multi-population longevity forecasting that embeds actuarial knowledge into LSTM training through differentiable penalty terms. Applied to a high-longevity 6-country cluster (Switzerland, Sweden, Norway, West Germany, Netherlands, Japan; 1956-2020), the framework is a challenger to the Li-Lee benchmark and unconstrained neural approaches.
  Our central finding is that monotonicity constraint intensity lambda functions as a continuous governance dial with a quantifiable accuracy-stability trade-off. At lambda = 0.01, 30-year forecast confidence intervals narrow by 6.5% at zero RMSE cost. At lambda = 0.1, they narrow by 25% at only +0.84% RMSE cost. This trade-off is invisible to standard hyperparameter optimizers, which select lambda by minimizing one-step RMSE, the wrong metric for structural constraints in recursive forecasting.
  The framework adds three contributions: (i) residual-calibrated process noise that eliminates double-counting in the dual uncertainty framework, reducing confidence intervals by 53-60%; (ii) a 5-seed model ensemble with a coefficient of variation of 1.06%; and (iii) a time-varying credibility weight Z(t) = exp(-alpha t) connecting to Buhlmann credibility theory for blending neural and actuarial predictions. A 10-year out-of-sample backtest (trained on 1956-2010, validated against observed HMD life expectancy for 2011-2020) yields a mean absolute error of 0.38 years, with 11 of 12 country x sex combinations within the 90% confidence interval. The model produces regulatory-grade outputs including Solvency Capital Requirements under the Swiss Solvency Test (ES 99.0%: +1.91 years, CHE Male) and Solvency II, reverse stress testing, and model-based stability verification (amplification ratio 1.02x).

title: Clustering-Based Artificial Tree Ensembles for Random Forest Approximation
summary:
arXiv:2611.18803v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Random Forests (RFs) offer strong prediction performance but are difficult to interpret. Most representative trees (MRTs) and artificial representative trees (ARTs) provide surrogate explanations, but a single tree may miss patterns within a forest. We investigate benefits and limitations of clustering-based representative tree ensembles for RF surrogate modeling and assess the contribution of similarity-based clustering relative to random tree partitions. Using linear and nonlinear simulations and regression benchmarks, we evaluate fidelity, prediction accuracy, complexity, and prediction stability against equally sized ensembles of top-ranked MRTs and randomly selected trees. Increasing ensemble size generally improves fidelity, accuracy, and prediction stability. ART ensembles show higher fidelity in simulations and often greater prediction stability for small ensembles. Compared with random tree partitions, similarity-based clustering generally improves ART fidelity in simulations and often on benchmarks. On benchmark datasets, MRT-based ensembles generally achieve higher fidelity and prediction accuracy, whereas ART ensembles have fewer terminal nodes. ART ensembles provide compact surrogates when reduced complexity matters and their fidelity and prediction accuracy meet application requirements. These findings clarify both the trade-offs of representative tree ensembles as RF surrogates and the contribution of similarity-based clustering beyond random clustering.
